subtopic: DETAILS OF OLDER WORKER INCENTIVE TRAINING PROGRAM

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: DETAILS OF OLDER WORKER INCENTIVE TRAINING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to announce the details of an older worker employment and training incentive program which will become effective on November 1, 1963.
The duration of unemployment for workers over 45 is generally much longer than for younger workers. The government has therefore initiated this program which is designed to assist long term unemployed mature men and women to re-enter employment and secure necessary skills. This plan involves incentive payments to employers to hire eligible older workers between November 1, 1963 and January 31, 1964. The payments will amount to 50 per cent of the monthly wage paid, or $75 per month, whichever is less. The program will assist employers during the period in which an eligible older worker is being given the training and work experience necessary for his continued employment.
The conditions governing the payment of incentives to employers are as follows:
1.	Incentive payments apply only to employment which is insurable under the Unemployment Insurance Act, excluding employment by governments at all levels and by government owned business enterprises.
2.	The employer must provide the worker with a significant amount of approved on the job training or, if this is inappropriate, other approved programs to assist the worker to continue in gainful employment.
3.	The employer must hire the worker during the period November 1, 1963 to January 31, 1964 and employ the worker or his eligible replacement for at least three months before the incentive becomes payable.
4.	The worker must not be employed in a job vacated by another worker after September 1, 1963.
The conditions applying to the eligibility of workers for employment under the program are as follows:
1- The worker must be 45 years of age or over and not in full time employment at the time of hiring.
2.	The worker must not be eligible for regular unemployment insurance benefits.
3.	The worker must have been unemployed for at least six of the previous nine months. Evidence of unemployment can be provided by registration with the national employment service, receipt of unemployment assistance payments or other satisfactory evidence of attachment to the labour market.
4.	The worker must not be in receipt of the universal old age pension or any other retirement or pension benefits equivalent to or higher than the amount of universal old age pension.
5.	The worker must be the only member of the family household for whom an incentive payment is made.
I might add that the national employment service will be responsible for the implementation of the program at the community level. The Department of Labour will be responsible for the general promotion of the program itself.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this announcement by the Minister of Labour is a further example of the way in which the present government, having made policy announcements well in advance, comes out with the working details of those policies only 24 days or so before those policies are to be put into effect. In other words it has been the habit of this government to announce policies without working out their details; and even when the details have been worked out, it has been evident that those policies do not operate in the way which was intended.
This incentive of $75 per month to employers who employ workers of 45 years of age and over from November 1, 1963 to January 31, 1964 is an attempt to encourage the hiring of these older workers. The period for which they will be hired is another matter. The duration of their employment is a vital matter, and it should not be on a temporary basis; it should be done on a permanent basis. When the former government, the Conservative government, was in office our concern was for the older worker and his employment, as was the concern of everyone in this country. We endeavoured, through an educational process, to acquaint employers with the ability and dependability of the older worker. In this effort we were successful to a considerable extent.
It now remains to be seen whether this new gimmick for the employment of the older worker will work out as well as it is hoped, or intended, it will, or whether it will

Last week I asked for further enlightenment in that connection.
The Minister of Labour informs us today that the assistance will start on November 1,
1963,	and will continue up to January 31,
1964,	that is over a period of three months. During that time, employers of workers 45 years of age or over who were previously unemployed will be entitled to an allowance of 50 per cent of the salaries paid up to a maximum of $75 a month.
In his statement, the minister referred to the fact that employers will have to prove that they will provide the training required to enable those unemployed to keep their new jobs. Such a condition, I must say, will probably be exceedingly difficult to control.
What kind of training will be considered as required for an employer to be entitled to that special payment? What, in the minister's view, constitutes training capable of helping a man keep a job after three months?
Can we consider that somebody who has been previously unemployed for six months will be able to benefit from the training as set forth in the act?
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, that is one of the points which will be eagerly discussed and with which some might play politics, something which I for one deplore at this time.
I am of the opinion that the civil servants who will have to decide who is entitled to that grant and who is not, will find themselves in a very difficult situation and even liable to make unfair decisions.
I feel that point had to be raised and I hope the minister, in a further statement, will be able to clarify what will be considered sufficient training to enable employers to benefit from that allowance.
I said last week that those measures were good in themselves but were still only of a temporary nature and that nothing would really solve the problem facing young people and those not so young as long as the economy is not moving again and does not improve enough to offer employment to all those who are looking for work.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: SHIPPING INDUSTRY
subsubtopic: RESPECTING VACATION PAY ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to advise the house that I have revoked the approval previously given under the Annual Vacations Act to vacation pay arrangements contained in collective agreements between the seafarers international union and a large number of shipping companies.
Where approval is given such collective agreement arrangements, the act no longer has application. With the revocation of approval in these cases the act will now apply and employers in the shipping industry will henceforth pay vacation pay direct to employees instead of to the S.I.U.
It will also be recalled that Mr. Justice Norris found that the conditions laid down in granting approval had not been fulfilled by the S.I.U. and the shipping companies.
Detailed directions in this regard have gone out to the trade union and the great lakes shipping companies concerned.

subtopic: MOTION TO SUSPEND ADJOURNMENT TIME AND TO PERMIT SEVERAL READINGS OF SUPPLY BILL
speechtext:
That, until the proceedings on the interim supply resolution, now before the house, and on the supply bill to be based thereon have been disposed of, the provisions of section 3 of standing order 6 concerning the time of evening adjournment shall be suspended; and that, in order to allow for several readings of the said supply bill in any sitting, the provisions of standing order 75 shall be suspended in relation thereto;
Provided that, if any other government order is taken in any such sitting, the terms of this order shall not be operative.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with the very-greatest reluctance that I rise this afternoon to propose the motion standing in my name on the order paper. I think all of us are perhaps more sensible than we have been for quite a long time that the eyes of the whole country are upon this house at this time; and I think most of us, at any rate, feel that the electorate, regardless of party, expect us first of all to discharge the business of the public.
Now, it is well known that we have before us, or will have before us when the orders of the day are reached today, the resumption of the debate on interim supply. It is known that there are peculiar procedural and other difficulties that could arise in the discussion of interim supply. As successive governments have often reminded the house, it has usually been possible to deal with interim supply fairly quickly. However, there have been times when that has not been possible.
It does seem to me that there were somewhat unusual circumstances in this particular case, because the house had recessed for the best part of two months and there was a resumption of a session in which there were a number of questions of real moment and concern. The interim supply debate went on for two days last week, and not one word of exception was taken from this side of the house to that fact. No attempt of any kind was made to restrict that debate in any way. In fact several members of the government, notably the Minister of Labour, took part in that debate. There was, therefore, an effort on the part of the government to deal with matters relating to public business that were raised during those two days. Moreover, sir, it had been the intention of the government, had interim supply been granted on Friday, to have a supply motion today which would have provided every opportunity to hon. members to air any grievances that might have arisen against the government in the conduct of public business.
At the end of two days of debate on Friday there was a disposition in the committee, if I understood it right-I am not relying on my own memory, but I am relying on the words of certain hon. gentlemen opposite-to grant supply. I should like to refer very briefly to what was said by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, as recorded at page 3236 of Hansard:
Mr. Chairman, it is now five o'clock and I wonder if I could suggest that we obtain unanimous consent to continuing in committee through the next hour, which would give an opportunity to those hon. members of the house who have a special interest in prolonging this debate to exhaust all their presentations to the committee.
So far as I could judge this was acceptable to everyone then present in the committee with the exception of one hon. member, who
Suspension of Adjournment Time exercised his undoubted rights under the rules to object. Then the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre made what I thought was an admirable and responsible intervention. At a later stage, when we had taken up the private business and the order had been called for second reading of a bill relating to sweepstakes, standing in the name of the hon. member for Acadia, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre said, as recorded on page 3239 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, may I break the rules by interrupting at this point? We have been proceeding rather quickly. As I understand the house leader, he suggested that if we were not going ahead with the bill recently dealt with, we might stand other public bills and go back into committee of supply if he could have an assurance from this side that we and other members of other parties would stand our bills. I presume our people would be willing to do that.
I think the hon. gentleman was speaking for his party, as the evidence showed a few minutes later. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre almost immediately afterward said this:
Mr. Speaker, we would be very happy to comply with this suggestion. Progress should be made on the interim supply bill and, if possible, with the old age pensions as well.
Why then, sir, in view of this almost universal evidence of co-operation and willingness to dispose of the matter, should there be any excuse whatever for bringing on this motion at the present time? I think I have to found that upon a statement made by the hon. member for Lapointe the evening before. It will be found at page 3197 of Hansard for Thursday, October 3, in which the hon. member said:
Mr. Chairman, I must inform you that we do not intend to end the debate on interim supply either tonight, tomorrow or as long as the privileges and elections committee has not remedied the ridiculous and illogical situation which prevails in this corner of the house. We tried to do it and it was supposed to be done as soon as possible. Last Monday, the house asked that the situation be settled but it has not yet been done.
Then on Friday the hon. gentleman said, as reported at page 3212 of Hansard:
It rests with certain members of the government to see that a decision is taken as soon as possible, because it is absolutely illogical and utterly ridiculous not to recognize a group of 13 members...
and he continued from there. I think the hon. gentleman on reflection-and I know he will reflect on this-will realize that this is not, and under our rules cannot be, a matter for the government. The whole house accepted a motion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, on the day the session resumed, to remit the matter of the seating in the house to a committee; and under our rules, while that committee is deliberating

Suspension of Adjournment Time it is contrary to the rules for the matter to be debated here in the house.
I do not intend to debate it but merely to draw attention to the tact; that the house, by a decision which no hon. member opposed, remitted this matter to the committee, and until it comes back from the committee the house has not power, under its rules, to deal with the matter. Moreover, the friends of the government are not a majority on that committee or any other committee of the house, any more than the government itself has a majority in the house, so that it is quite impossible for the government as a government to settle this matter. It is a matter for the house. It is a matter, as Your Honour properly pointed out, of the organization of the house; and whatever the disposition of the government might be it is not within its power under our constitution, and it would be an attempt to usurp powers the government has not got and has not the right to have, to attempt to settle any question which is a question for the whole house.
Therefore it seems to me, sir, it is rather illogical to hold up the business of the country because a committee of the house has not yet been able to discharge an obligation placed upon it. I believe there are other ways under our rules by which one can air a grievance against a committee, but to hold up supply in the house would not, it seems to me, be a very effective remedy in that regard.
On Friday, as reported at page 3244 of Hansard for that day, when asked to announce the business of the house for this week by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre I pointed out;
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it would be very wise for me on this occasion to attempt to forecast the business very far ahead, because until interim supply has been granted it will of course not be possible, I am afraid, to do any other business at all. Therefore that will be the first item of business on Monday.
I think it is only fair to hon. members in all parts of the house for me to indicate as briefly and as clearly as I can just what is the degree of urgency of the public business. I am informed by the officials of the treasury that there are already bills which ought to be paid by the government and which are unpaid because the house has not yet seen fit to vote the supply necessary to make it possible to pay them. I am also informed that unless this grant of interim supply can be made by the end of the day tomorrow-and that means dealing with the matter in both houses, securing the royal assent and then having the supply released by the governor in council-certain of the cheques for the payment of public servants which normally go out in the middle of the month and which are normally spread over three days at the
middle of the month-which process is affected to some degree by the fact that Monday next is Thanksgiving day and a bank holiday-and which would normally be received by public servants on Thursday, cannot be given to them because the money will not be available; and that for every day's delay the number of public servants so affected will be greater.
I am also advised that unless this house and the other place are able later this week or, at the very latest, at the beginning of next week to deal with all stages of the amendment to the Old Age Security Act, it will not be practical to include the additional payment in the cheques which are normally received, I believe, in all parts of Canada by the recipients on the twentieth day of the month. Therefore it is a matter of some urgency which will affect a great number of our fellow citizens. It is for that reason, and for that reason alone, that the government has felt that in view of the statement made in the house by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), assuming he was speaking for those associated with him in making that statement, we should take every step it was reasonably possible to take under the rules to make as sure as we could that these bills would be paid. Of course we are in the hands of the house; we cannot do more than accept what the majority of hon. members wish to have done in this matter, but we thought we should take every feasible step to see that ample time was available for hon. members to air any additional grievances they might feel they had and still enable the house and the whole parliament to discharge its duties and to enable the fundamental business of the country, the public business, to go on.
I cannot believe, sir, that the country really would feel that this house was justified or that any part of the house was justified in holding up the public business, the business of all the people of Canada, because anybody in any part of the house was not satisfied with the place in which he happened temporarily to be sitting, particularly when a procedure had been provided whereby this question could be settled. This is a question which has some real complications in it, as I think all of us with any sense of the history of parliament realize, and the house has already provided unanimously for another way of dealing with that question.
Therefore, sir, it seemed to us that there was no real choice in the circumstances but to put forward this motion, the more so when one considers the exchange which took place between myself and the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Plourde) on Friday afternoon. I would like also to put that on the record. When the hon. member for Quebec West rose to speak, he was good enough to

let me interrupt him, and I made this statement:
I wonder if hon. members would permit me to say just a word? I think all hon. members should be aware, if they are not already, of the fact we are on an interim supply motion. This is the fourth day of October, a Friday, and the next day that the house will be sitting will be the seventh. We are practically at the point where the government will not be able to pay the public servants or make other essential payments unless the business now before the committee is completed with very little delay. It had been the intention of the government, unless some emergency legislation was required, to have a supply motion on Monday, at which time all hon. members would have, as they always have, the greatest possible freedom of debate. I wondered, Mr. Chairman, if there was any possibility of bringing these proceedings to a conclusion now and dealing with the supply bill so that it could go to the other place and the ordinary business of the country could go on. It seems to me that if this could be done, anything that might be said on this motion could also be said on another occasion.
I am not seeking in any way to restrict hon. members, but I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, who was frequently in the position I am now in, is well aware of the urgency of this matter. I am not seeking to suggest in any way that the debate be restricted and I have no fault to find with any hon. member in any section of the house, because some very urgent matters have been discussed today and we recognize that these matters are urgent. But I thought it only right for me to bring the situation in which the whole house finds itself at the moment to the attention of the committee.
The deputy chairman then asked, "Shall the resolution carry?" and I think most hon. members who were here said "Carried". Then the hon. member for Quebec West said this:
I regret I cannot accept that proposal. When we are recognized in the house, we shall then be able to agree, but for the time being I must carry on with this debate on supply.
What does that statement mean? It means that the hon. gentleman said in effect that he had nothing more to say on supply and he would be prepared to agree to the supply but only if something else, that was not in the power of the committee of supply to do or that time in the power of the house to do, because it had been remitted to the committee on privileges and elections, had been done. It seems to me that on reflection all hon. members will realize that it will be a very serious thing for the public interest if a question of the mere internal organization of the house, the house-keeping of the house so to speak, should be put before the public business which we are elected to discharge. That, it seems to me, is the problem with which we are faced. It seems to me that the government, unpleasant as it is to ask hon. members to forego the usual adjournment and to prolong the debate, had no option in the circumstances, in view of the urgency of the public business which I have sought to state in as accurate and as temperate a manner as possible, but to bring this motion before the house.
Suspension of Adjournment Time
I may say that if the government at this stage could receive satisfactory assurances that before ten o'clock today the interim supply could be concluded, I would be very happy indeed to ask the house to permit this motion to stand. But in default of those assurances it seems to me-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is one of the historic days in the Commons of Canada. We have now seen the spectacle of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) and government house leader coming before the house in sackcloth and ashes to ask forgiveness for his sins of the past. This is the most amazing development in the 12 years that I have been here in the House of Commons. Apparently if you wait long enough things happen which change the course of history, and sinners finally repent. So we have today the house leader, the arranger of government business, the man behind the scenes who fixes things up-the "grey eminence" as we used to call him in years gone by before he entered the government-now trying, in his capacity as house leader, to persuade the house to do, as he puts it, things which are solely for the good of the country. It is not the government which is so seriously concerned; it is the putting ahead of all other considerations for the good of the country.
This is a complete change in the character of my opposite number here, the government house leader. In all the years I have been here and that he has been in the house he has been working around this way and that, particularly when he was on the opposition side, to make it difficult for the government of that day to carry on. I had several years of that experience and I know whereof I speak. Now in sackcloth and ashes he comes here before us and says, in effect, that his plans have all failed; that it is not possible to organize the business of the house; that despite all his experience in the past and all the lectures which he gave me for about four years he now finds it impossible to organize the business of the house. We start with one subject matter; he then withdraws it, brings another bill before the house and has a go at that; and then changes around and brings on something else.
Perhaps the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) will also enter into this debate today. He was the champion last year of leadership and good government. He was telling us that if only we had leadership in this house and the business was properly organized we would get things done. This is the

Suspension oj Adjournment Time man who said: "Why don't you start with a bill and carry it right through to completion?" Well, he has now had an observance of another government in office with an experienced operator in charge of government business, and I hope that he will get up and say again that what we require in this house is leadership and a proper organization of the business, and that if we are going to start with something, that we stay with it and carry it through to completion. Because that has not been the case in this session.
Now, Mr. Speaker, how did all this trouble arise? The trouble arose through the fault of the government itself. The house leader has read to us the ultimatum which was delivered to the house on Thursday night by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). This took us by surprise, because the hon. member for Lapointe has so frequently been seen to cross over to get, as we always thought, instructions from the Secretary of State or people on that side of the house. We have seen messages apparently relayed to him on this side so that a question can be asked which is easily answered to the satisfaction of the originators of the question. Now, what has spoiled this friendship?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was hoping that with this reminder the hon. member for Lapointe would subsequently get into the debate and give us a statement with regard to what he is attempting to do in the House of Commons. I simply said that, as observers here, this is what we thought was going on, and that now what we had considered to be a beautiful friendship seems to have been destroyed. This disturbs us no end. How is the government going to be sustained in office if this beautiful friendship is destroyed? They may be forced out of office by these actions.
The ultimatum to which I have referred was given to us on Thursday night. The house leader has already drawn attention to it, but let us make sure of the words again. At page 3197 of Hansard the hon. member for Lapointe is reported as having said:
Mr. Chairman, I must inform you that we do not intend to end the debate on interim supply either tonight, tomorrow or as long as the privileges and elections committee has not remedied the ridiculous and illogical situation which prevails in this corner of the house.

And so, faced with this ultimatum, this is the response of the house leader. He says: "I cannot deal any longer with my former friend so now the house has to come to my rescue and we must sit night and day until those who wish to operate a filibuster in this house are worn out." This is the state of affairs at the present time.
The Secretary of State spoke about the urgency of this matter and told us that unless the interim supply is granted by Tuesday night very dire consequences will result. He pointed out that we have already had some time on interim supply and should now terminate the debate. He is constantly giving advice to the house as to what to do. Just the other day he wanted to have a committee set up without debate. He did not want debate in the house. Now he wants us to debate night and day, so I do not know what side he is on.
I think that the proper organization of the business of the house is to make arrangements, and confidential arrangements, so that when a controversial issue is coming before the house it may be possible for one spokesman for each party to speak on behalf of his party, and then the measure might well go through rather quickly. But he rises in the house and says: "I should like to bring this measure before you but I do not want any debate on it". What does he want? We now know that he wants to debate endlessly night and day all week. The hon. gentleman mentioned urgency. Unless this matter is settled by tomorrow night there will be difficulty, he said. Well, we have been all through this before. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, a diligent student of the House of Commons in the past, made a review in 1956 of interim supply procedure over many preceding years. I have done the same myself. In 1956, when a critical moment was approaching the House of Commons and when interim supply was up for consideration on June 11, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre recited for the benefit of the house the way in which interim supply had been dealt with over the years. Quite correctly, the Secretary of State has suggested that it can be dealt with very quickly on occasions, and the practice of the house normally has been to deal with interim supply very quickly, sometimes in 30 minutes, sometimes in an hour and a half, sometimes in half a day and sometimes in one day; the discussion rarely exceeds one day's sitting.
The urgency of such a motion has always been recognized by the House of Commons. It is important that the cheques go out to the people who are expecting their midmonth's salary, to those whom money is

owed by the government. As the Secretary of State has pointed out, there is an arrangement whereby the cheques, which are numerous, are spread over three days. I have talked over the years with members of my staff who have been drawing cheques of this nature and they say this three day period is normal. They can take their cheques down to the bank on the 13th, 14th and 15th of the month, if these are weekdays and the banks are not pressed; and the people who are cashing government cheques do not have to form longer queues than are now required. We recognize the urgency of this matter but it is strange that in 1956 interim supply was passed on June 11 without serious objection being taken and I think we will be able to find other instances when interim supply was passed as late in the month as that. However, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out in his survey in 1956, it has been customary for the house to deal with interim supply about two weeks before the cheques are required, in other words, toward the end of the month.
I thought that when we reassembled a week ago the first item to be considered would be interim supply which, perhaps, would have gone through in 20 or 30 minutes. But it was postponed until Thursday. Despite the urgency which the leader of the house draws to our attention he failed, it seems, to remind the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) of the object he had in mind. The Secretary of State for External Affairs intervened in the debate on interim supply in order to make a statement regarding his particular problems related to external affairs. Would it not have been better to have arranged for a special debate on external afEairs early in the session, as has been requested by hon. members on this side of the house, rather than to have had the Secretary of State for External Affairs intervene on Thursday to make a speech dealing with one of the most controversial subjects which has been before the House of Commons in years. Then, I presume, other hon. members were not to reply. The hon. gentleman has spoken, and that is the end of the debate. I should have liked to take part in that debate on external affairs and to have answered some of the questions put forward by the minister. I should have liked to take up his statement that Canada is now in a stronger position to favour disarmament, because she has nuclear arms on her soil.
Hon. members will appreciate the range of subjects which are opened up by the intervention of ministers other than the Minister of Finance. Interim supply should be carried on by the Minister of Finance. The leader of the house should absent himself and other
Suspension of Adjournment Time ministers should remain silent. Then something would be done and the urgency of the matter would be met. Why did not the leader of the house speak to his colleagues and tell them: keep out of this debate, let the opposition people speak and we shall get the measure through. He did not adopt that course.
As a matter of fact, the cheques for those who are expecting payments by the government could be cashed on the 15th of this month, that is, on Tuesday of next week. Monday, of course, is Thanksgiving day, and there is, of course, Saturday and Sunday. If the normal practice were followed, the cheques could be cashed on Thursday and Friday of this week and the following Tuesday. I doubt very much if anybody will be seriously inconvenienced if the cheques are not cashed until Friday or the following Tuesday. They are dated the 15th of the month. The banks, relying on the government, will, I am told, accept them a day or two in advance. However, the Secretary of State tells us that unless we deal with this matter by tomorrow night, people are going to be seriously inconvenienced. I wonder if that is completely accurate. Granted there has been a three day period for the cashing and distribution of these cheques in the light of the difficulties which confront this house perhaps the cashing of the cheques could be done in two days rather than in three or, at the worst, on the day on which they fall due, which is the 15th. I should much prefer the matter to be dealt with more expeditiously and in a more orderly fashion, but I question the statement of the Secretary of State that this matter must be settled by Tuesday night.
I would say the wrong method of dealing with interim supply was indicated to this house last year by the Liberal party which now forms the government. During the course of last session alone, just consider the delays which were involved. Hon. members can look at the whole calendar year, 1962, and they will find that in the closing weeks of that session-and the house was dissolved in April-the opposition took 27 days discussing supplementary estimates which were just a continuation of the main estimates. That had never been done before in the House of Commons. Considerations of urgency they brushed aside. For 27 days they continued to discuss expenditures which they had been discussing earlier when the main estimates were before the house.
Then, after the election of 1962, when the house resumed in the fall of 1962, what did they do? Talk about urgency in granting supply. They blocked everything we brought before this house in the way of supply. We had a supply motion and six departments were called. Not one item of the estimates

Suspension of Adjournment Time for 1962 was passed by the House of Commons: Not one item. Yet the Department of Agriculture was before the house for three days. Other departments were called and dealt with. But their estimates were not passed-not one single item.
Then, as to interim supply, we called for interim supply in December last year. This government, if it survives, will be calling for interim supply in December of this year and if we grant the present supply motion for which they are asking they will have had interim supply for eight months.
We will hear from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) about giving the government a blank cheque for a period of eight months with no estimates having been passed by the house except those of the Department of Trade and Commerce, which I arranged by asking Conservative members on this side to refrain from lengthy debate. Those estimates were passed. The estimates of the Department of Transport were almost finished and we also started on the estimates of the Department of Finance. But last session not a single estimate was passed and interim supply was asked for. Now it is being requested for a period of eight months. A blank cheque is being sought and two thirds of all estimates for the fiscal year are being voted in this way without careful consideration, item by item.
Those are the arguments that were used against us last fall. In December of last year when we asked the house to vote interim supply for the month of January the members of the Liberal opposition were fully familiar with the urgency of interim supply. They knew how urgent it was and that the voting of money was required to carry on the normal business of the country, to provide for the pay cheques of people who were on the government payroll and to pay debts and things of that nature. Despite their knowledge of the urgency they took seven days, Mr. Speaker, to pass interim supply.

He said at that time, and these words are worth recording:
Theoretically there were these two choices_
Applying closure or dissolving parliament. He only had two choices in January, 1963, applying closure or dissolving parliament, but now he has come up with a third-sit night and day. These are his words:
Theoretically, there were these two choices, but in fact there was not. The government had been deeply wounded by the battle over the use of closure in the pipe line debate. Notwithstanding the fact that the pipe line debate had lasted a full month, the opposition had succeeded in creating the impression that freedom of speech was being denied and that the ministers were riding roughshod over parliament. To impose closure on the debate on a supply bill would have been to limit the right of the Commons to control the expenditures of the crown and the Liberal government was not, in fact, prepared even to consider closure as a possible course of action. Moreover, if closure had been tried, it would have required nearly two weeks to secure the passage of the bill, the public servants would have gone without pay, and other urgent expenditures could not have been made. All the opposition had to do in the week of June 11, 1956, was to go on debating the government's expenditures for three or four days and the government would have been forced to ask for a dissolution of parliament and an election.

There is the mentor. That is the way you do it. In February of last winter that is what they were prepared to do. "Wait until interim supply comes up on Wednesday", said the then Leader of the Opposition, "and you are for it". Why are they delaying? This is what we would like to know. Let that committee decide, and then we will not have to go through this method, and this procedure, of sitting night and day to try to wear out some people who have a grievance against this government.
1 should like to propose a solution to this difficulty, Mr. Speaker, but before presenting

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that no member likes the idea of removing the hours of adjournment so that we face the prospect of sitting all night. Nevertheless I am prepared to support this motion if there is no other compromise that can be found so that the business of the country can be continued and certain important legislation, particularly that having to do with increasing old age pensions, can be dealt with at the earliest possible date.
Let us take a brief moment to see why we are in the situation in which we find ourselves. The supporters of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) feel they have a grievance with reference to their seating in the house, and their recognition as a political party or group. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I think this is an important question, and the members of the New Democratic party are also concerned about the question of seating in the house and recognition of priorities. That is why the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) a week ago today moved a motion to refer this matter to the committee on privileges and elections. That committee was only constituted last Thursday and it has not had very much time. I

Suspension of Adjournment Time would say to the hon. member for Villeneuve that if it becomes apparent that this committee is dragging its feet or that it is stalling or deliberately putting oil reaching a decision, we will be as active as any other members in raising the matter in the house and urging that the committee reach a decision and make a report to the house.
But I want to say to the hon. member for Villeneuve that surely the seating arrangements in this house, whether for the Cre-ditistes or for the New Democratic party, are relatively unimportant compared to the conduct of the public affairs of Canada. As my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, said last week in introducing his motion, it is an honour to sit in any part of this house, and while we will be just as zealous as any other group in asking that we be given proper recognition I do not think this justifies any group in the house, no matter how important they may think they are, being allowed to hold up interim supply and thereby making it impossible to meet accounts which are due.
What is just as serious, Mr. Speaker, is that by holding up interim supply we are holding up proceeding with the amendments to the Old Age Security Act. I think the house wasted three days last week discussing the resolution precedent to that bill. It could have been passed in a couple of hours but three days were lost. I want to point out that as far as this group is concerned we put up two speakers, both of whom spoke less than 10 minutes. We were prepared last Thursday to see the interim supply measure go through. We do not think that any group of members, on the basis of a personal grievance affecting their privileges in this house-not on a matter of policy, not on something which affects the welfare of Canada-has the right to stop the conduct of public affairs; and that is what holding up interim supply amounts to.
I want to make an appeal to the hon. member for Villeneuve and to those who are supporting him. After all, not only the eyes of Canada but the eyes of many countries are upon this democratic parliament. In the world in which we live democracy is on trial as it has not been for many decades. Democracy can be destroyed and discredited just as much by people from within as by its enemies from outside. The very essence of democracy is a capacity for self-discipline. The success of democracy depends upon the willingness of those who sit in parliament to forget their petty bickerings and partisan advantage wherever the public good is involved.
I would say that parliament is making a pretty poor spectacle of itself when interim supply is held up and when a bill to increase old age pensions is held up merely because

we in this corner of the house feel that we have a grievance about the seating arrangements, a matter which I might point out is already before a parliamentary committee and under consideration. I would therefore urge the supporters of the hon. member for Villeneuve to reconsider their attitude. I would urge them to consider the public image which we are creating for the people of Canada. If we are to restore people's faith in democratic procedures, I think it can only be done if the general public are convinced that this parliament is serious about conducting public affairs.
I am sorry the government did not give some consideration to the amendment which was moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, because I am not sure that removing the closing hours and sitting all night is necessarily going to push through interim supply. I suppose eventually, by a process of exhaustion, we will get interim supply through. But that is not a very happy way in which to conduct the affairs of this parliament. It seems to me that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre made an eminently sensible proposal. Your Honour has ruled the amendment out of order, and so I am not going to discuss it. But it seems to me if some agreement could be reached among the various parties, that the committee will sit while the house is sitting, that it will try, within 48 or 72 hours or a shorter time if possible, to bring down a report, then the hon. member for Villeneuve and his supporters could be assured that this committee is not going to drag out this matter for weeks or months or that this is simply a stalling device. If this course could be agreed to by the government, and the gentlemen who feel aggrieved are prepared at the same time to allow interim supply to go through, then we could get on with the business of the house.
I make an appeal to both the government and the Creditistes to get together to see if a compromise cannot be worked out. I am prepared to support this motion if it is the only alternative, but I am not sure, Mr. Speaker, that it will solve our problem. It will certainly mean that for the next 48 hours or so we will be sitting night and day listening to an interminable discussion, not by members who are objecting to some vote in the interim supply measure, but simply listening to speeches that are made for the purpose of holding up the business of the house. It seems to me that is not a spectacle that is likely to enhance the prestige of democracy either in Canada or in other parts of the world.
I do hope some agreement can be reached whereby the committee would undertake to meet while the house is sitting, and to bring down a report before the end of this week.

I hope, at the same time, the hon, member for Villeneuve and his supporters will agree to forgo the filibuster which they have threatened, and forgo the attempt to blackmail this house into bullying the committee into doing something it is not prepared to do. If they are prepared to make this kind of compromise, and the government is prepared to accept such a compromise, we can get on with the business of the house. speechtext:
What action, in detail, has been taken with respect to each of the following recommendations of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Indian affairs:
"(a) The question of transferring health services for Indians to the provinces should be discussed at a dominion-provincial conference, but the present health program should be continued and extended until such time as this can be accomplished.

(b)	Provincial welfare legislation and services should be used for the benefit of the Indian population.
(c)	Social welfare should be placed on the agenda of a dominion-provincial conference with a view to transferring jurisdiction to the provinces.
(d)	A substantially increased public investment should be made in Indian housing and sanitation facilities.
(e)	A revolving loan fund for housing purposes should be established."?

1960-	61	$21,066,9581961-	62	22,127,3611962-	63	23,083,1381963-	64	23,479,215(b)	It is the policy and practice to use provincial welfare legislation and services for Indians wherever possible. Welfare services and social benefits available to Indians, other than those financed entirely by Indian affairs branch or through band funds, are provided from one of two sources:
(i) welfare programs developed through cooperative cost-sharing arrangements with provincial, municipal and private organizations; and (ii) welfare programs operated by other federal and provincial departments of government.
Categorical assistance
Indians are eligible for family allowances and old age security administered by the federal government as well as for old age assistance, blind and disabled persons' allowances administered by provincial governments.
In Ontario and Quebec, Indian women receive mothers' allowances on the same basis as non-Indian mothers. Under the Nova Scotia assistance program, Indian mothers and abandoned Indian children are recipients of provincial social assistance.
Public assistance
In Quebec there has been some experimentation with the inclusion of Indians in an over-all assistance program.
Under the Ontario general welfare assistance act, 33 Indian bands (about half the Indian population of Ontario) participate in the provincial welfare assistance program.
In Saskatchewan, all provincial welfare services are available to Indians living off reserves.
Questions
The province of British Columbia provides welfare assistance to Indians, who are living off reserves and who have not established residence in a municipality, on a refundable basis from Indian affairs branch.
Child welfare
As the field of child welfare is a provincial responsibility, there is a variance from one province to another in the administration and financing of the child care programs. In all provinces, Indian affairs branch assumes responsibility for the maintenance of Indian children under the care and supervision of the child welfare agency.
In British Columbia, Alberta, Quebec and Prince Edward Island, child welfare services are available to all children of the province on the same basis.
An agreement between the federal and British Columbia governments provides for a federal contribution toward the administrative costs of two social workers employed full time among the Indian population in the Smithers and Prince Rupert areas.
Child welfare services in Saskatchewan are extended to Indian reserves on a very limited referral basis from Indian affairs branch to the provincial department of child welfare.
An agreement between the federal government and the children's aid societies of western Manitoba provides for the extension of child welfare services to the reserves within the area of jurisdiction of the children's aid societies of western Manitoba.
Child welfare services are available to all reserves in Ontario through agreements with the federal government and the children's aid societies.
In New Brunswick, certain children's aid societies have provided limited child welfare services on reserves; however, there is no agreement with the provincial government and/or societies.
An agreement between the government of Nova Scotia and the federal government allows for the extension of child welfare services to all Nova Scotia reserves.
The federal and Yukon territorial governments have an agreement whereby the territorial government assumes responsibility for the administration of child welfare services and the federal government makes a financial contribution toward the administrative costs.
The department has an arrangement with northern affairs by which child welfare services and professional consultative services in all aspects of welfare in the district of Mackenzie are provided by northern affairs and national resources.

subtopic: SURVEYS RESPECTING CAESIUM 137 LEVELS
SURVEYS RESPECTING CAESIUM 137 LEVELS
speechtext:
1.	Has the government any information concerning the results of surveys conducted by U.S. health authorities in Alaska and, if so, (a) what was the nature of such results and (b) what level of caesium 137 was found by surveys?
2.	Is the federal government conducting similar surveys among Eskimos in northern Canada and, if so, (a) have any preliminary results been received and (b) has any comparison been made between U.S. results and any Canadian results?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SURVEYS RESPECTING CAESIUM 137 LEVELS
speechtext:
1. Yes. The results indicate that the levels of caesium 137 in Alaskan Eskimos who feed largely on caribou and reindeer meat are higher than those found elsewhere in Alaska or in the rest of the United States. Whole body counting measurements of caesium 137 in adult Alaskan Eskimos in 1962 ranged from 3 to 790 nanocuries. The highest observed level is less than the level recommended by the international commission on radiological protection as a basis for health assessment for individuals within the population. The highest average level for any community was 421 nanocuries. Typical levels in adults in other parts of the United States in 1962 were 5 to 7 nanocuries.
2. Yes. A study of fall-out levels in northern Canada has been initiated. This is a co-operative project involving units of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the Department of National Health and Welfare. The study is composed of a number of related but separate surveys. To date no direct measurements of caesium 137 in Canadian Eskimos have been made by whole body counting. Arrangements have however been made for such measurements. Urine specimens are being collected now and will be measured to give an indication of average caesium 137 levels in people in different communities. Samples of caribou and reindeer meat are also being received and measured for caesium 137; it is hoped that the first report on these measurements will be available in about a month. Levels of

caesium 137 in Canadians living in the more populated parts of Canada were about the same as those found in the United States during 1962.

speechtext:
1.	Does the government of Canada intend to maintain its preferential tariff policy for the republic of South Africa even if that country has withdrawn from the commonwealth?

There is no specific figure available on what percentage of South African exports to Canada enjoy tariff preferences. However, in 1962 of the nine leading South African exports to Canada valued at $12 million, $6.5 million or 54 per cent entered under a preferential tariff.

subsubtopic: REPORT RESPECTING INVISIBLE TRADE BARRIERS
speechtext:
1. Has the government's attention been drawn to the report on invisible trade barriers between

Canada and the United States recently published under the sponsorship of the Canadian-American committee?
2.	Is the government presently investigating the extent to which trade liberalization in Canada and the U.S.A. may be limited by (a) discretionary authority given customs officials to value and classify imports (b) interpretation by such officials of escape clauses in trade agreements (c) administrative zeal in restricting imports in ways not sanctioned by law?
3.	Briefly, what plan does the government have to deal with the problems raised by the above mentioned report?
Answer: 1. Yes. The government is aware of this publication by the Canadian-American committee of the national planning association (U.S.A.) and the private planning association of Canada.
2.	The government considers any subjects bearing on trade liberalization, on a continuing basis and as a matter of day to day business. There is no special investigation being conducted in respect of the points mentioned in the question. As regards (a) procedures are available in both countries to consult the customs authorities about value and classification problems, to seek a review, and to appeal decisions of officials. As regards (b), the invocation of escape clause procedures of international agreements would be a matter to be decided by the government in Canada; under United States law decisions on these matters are made by the president, after a report by the U.S. tariff commission has been made. As regards (c), it is of course the case that the laws of a sovereign country must be administered. As indicated above, established appeal procedures are available.
3.	Invisible barriers to Canadian exports, or non-tariff barriers as they are called, are a matter of interest and concern wherever they exist. We are continuing to press for removal of such barriers in our international trade consultations with other countries. The subject of non-tariff barriers to trade will be considered at the GATT trade conference next year.

Winter Navigation on St. Lawrence SHIPPING

speakeroldname: Mr. Thomas M. Bell (Saint John-Albert) moved:
subtopic: *TRIP TO WINDSOR BY EXTERNAL AFFAIRS MINISTER
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INQUIRY INTO WINTER NAVIGATION ON ST. LAWRENCE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, it is expedient that Her Majesty's government consider the advisability of appointing commissioners under Part I of the Inquiries Act:
(a)	to inquire into the extent of winter navigation on the St. Lawrence river and its effect on the Atlantic provinces;
(b)	to determine whether such action is in accord with the original spirit and mutual pledges of co-operation in which confederation was conceived;
(c)	to make such recommendations as they deem appropriate having regard to forging a dynamic national policy with particular respect to air, sea and land transportation in which the future of every region will be fully utilized with maximum benefits to that region.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this private members' notice of motion has been drafted a little wider than might have been necessary. In essence it simply deals with the effect of winter navigation on the ports of Saint John and Halifax. I have brought it under the Inquiries Act because of the present aversion to royal commissions. It is not inappropriate, either, that we should be discussing the St. Lawrence at the present time, in view of the problems that exist there. This matter has not been debated to any great extent through the years. There has been some discussion on the estimates of the Department of Transport and a few questions have been asked in the house from time to time, but I find no complete record of a full debate. I approach this matter, Mr. Speaker, in a nonpartisan way, and I understand that the hon. member for Halifax, and others, will be joining in this debate. I want to point out at the beginning that we in the maritimes do not stand in the way of progress: we, ourselves simply do not wish to be paying for this progress.
Some history should be placed on record in connection with this matter. We could go back to confederation to find various statements that were made at that time about the importance of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and their ports, and how they should be considered in any plans that might be put into effect in 1867. Sir John A. Macdonald is on record as having referred to this matter. I came across a very pertinent excerpt from the pre-confederation debates of 1865, in the provincial parliament of Canada, in Quebec, third session, page 349. Mr. Joly, the member for Lotbiniere, in speaking about Sir Etienne Tache, the president of the council, said this:
The honourable president of the council tells us that he is favourable to confederation, because it
[Mr. Speaker.!
will give us a seaport at all seasons of the year- a most powerful argument, he adds, in its favour. We stand in great need of a seaport in the winter season, more especially if the United States abolish the right of transit. Absolutely, without reference to that, we require it in order to perfect our system of defence.
Various statements have been made by people through the years about this matter. I recall the late Mr. Clarence Gillis, at one time a member from Cape Breton, was always a strong advocate about the problems that would be presented with the St. Lawrence seaway. In fact, in the light of the remarks made recently about maritimers by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), I often wish Mr. Gillis was with us in the house again, because he certainly would have dealt with the hon. member from his own party in his own strong way. Mr. Rand Matheson of the maritime transport commission always had fears in the early days of the seaway that when business was taken inland it would mean a greater use of the St. Lawrence in the summer. I recall Mr. Sam Balcom, a former member for Halifax, who on many occasions tabled questions about this matter, and Mr. Yvon Tasse, who was a member from Quebec, was also a great advocate of winter shipping in the city of Quebec.
We pointed out to him on many occasions that his difficulty in promoting the port of Quebec in the wintertime was that once Quebec was fully open the traffic would go past the door and on to Three Rivers and Montreal. I only mentioned these names, Mr. Speaker, to show that there has been some interest in this question, although there have not been any recorded debates. I mentioned this matter in the house on June 11, 1954, and the minister of transport at that time, now the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier), said:
I can tell my hon. friend that I cannot see any possibility of keeping the St. Lawrence route open during 12 months of the year. Certainly there is nothing envisaged in the plans for the development of the seaway, either jointly or separately, in connection with power and navigation, which would have anything to do with that subject either directly or indirectly. I do not foresee that in the immediate future, unless it be by atomic power, with which I am not competent to deal, there is any possibility of a longer season of navigation on the St. Lawrence.
Mr. Speaker, that brings the matter up to date. The icebreaking continues and we in Saint John and Halifax are faced each year during the winter season with the headlines of the newspapers that plague us incessantly. I have just copied some newspaper headlines to give the house an idea of the apprehension that exists in our minds. "Eleven icebreakers for St. Lawrence"; "More icebreakers urged for gulf"; "Labour protests

policy on Quebec icebreaker"; "Halifax becoming 'ghost town' port". These, I may interject, are headlines from Halifax and Saint John newspapers. Then "Montreal winter shipping-'feasible sooner or later' "Testing methods of removing ice"; "Icebound ship set free". That was on the St. Lawrence. "Nova Scotia port union boss says icebreakers shortening season"; "Year-around route stimulates industry-$100 million Levis development"; "Icebreakers have busy gulf season", and so on.
In order to prove my case conclusively, Mr. Speaker, I have some official figures published by the dominion bureau of statistics which show the traffic which has been built up at the ports of Quebec, Three Rivers and Montreal in January, February and March, the full winter season, from 1958 to 1963. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, and the permission of the house I would like to have this brief table printed in Hansard.

speechtext:
This matter has been presented on many occasions. The last formal time I recall its being raised was in a brief to the former minister of transport on May 30, 1961. This was a brief presented by the ports of Halifax and Saint John. It was most constructive. I refer to the part at the end of their brief where they dealt with the test of this matter of icebreaking and said:
The question should not be where the icebreaker is working, but what it is doing and whether the results meet an essential public need or national interest; or maybe whether the results are to some extent contrary to national interest and policy.
Winter Navigation on St. Lawrence
Certain representations were made in Saint John and Halifax to the MacPherson royal commission, but they felt that the terms of reference did not include a treatment of this subject. While there was a veiled reference in volume 2 of the MacPherson report there was not anything of a helpful nature in so far as concerns this matter which looms so large to these ports.
We were encouraged, however, when recently the Atlantic development board accepted as one of their first projects this entire subject. The former member for Halifax, Bob McCleave, was aggressive in his approaches to the Atlantic development board, as it was newly constitued and they accepted, as I say, a full study of this matter. I notice that this is to be continued by the new directors who made a statement on September 27, 1963, to the effect that the Atlantic development board will continue the economic examination of the effect on Atlantic ports, of winter shipping in the St. Lawrence seaway, and a scientific and engineering study of winter shipping in the St. Lawrence. This will be carried out together with existing studies that are being made by the national harbours board, and others.
I feel that one should be constructive about a matter such as this. I have jotted down a few questions that the Atlantic development board and others interested in this matter might wish to consider. First of all, will the ice in the straits still be a danger, even with icebreaking in the St. Lawrence? What is the threat from fresh water ice in the spring? Would all the winter traffic figures for the St. Lawrence be business that would otherwise have come to Saint John and Halifax? Has any activity that formerly went through American ports been diverted to any Canadian ports because of winter navigation? Have insurance rates changed in any way to spread extra costs for winter navigation over all ports of eastern Canada? Has export business been held up in the spring in order to wait for the opening of the St. Lawrence; and also, are orders rushed through Montreal in the fall before closing? Has there been any actual benefit to Halifax from the opening of Quebec in the winter as suggested? Is it possible to assess the costs of icebreaking even in a general way? If the St. Lawrence were navigable all year, would any legitimate new business be created that does not presently exist?
I throw those thoughts out, Mr. Speaker, and in addition suggest that some of the solutions might be of this nature. First, special costs assessed to shipping companies varied to the thickness of ships' plates, as in many northern European countries such as Finland.

Winter Navigation on St. Lawrence Second, individual icebreaker service should be paid for when and if needed. And third- and this is the suggestion that meets with more favour from responsible bodies in the maritimes-set freight rates on a directly competitive basis with the St. Lawrence; that is to say, with no advantage to the St. Lawrence, at least in wintertime. This equalization would, of course, be in the nature of a direct subsidy. It would be interesting to compare the estimates of these subsidy proposals with that of the entire cost of icebreaking services throughout the winter season on the St. Lawrence. Those are some solutions.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I merely say that this is a fast-moving transportation world. We are very apprehensive in Saint John and Halifax. I am speaking particularly from a Saint John standpoint when I say that we were at one time the fourth largest city in Canada, and probably the largest port at the time of confederation. We have many problems. We have a transit type of port activity, and the St. Lawrence would take more from us than Halifax. We are primarily serviced by Canadian Pacific. They are changing their passenger plans and making many other different moves, especially with regard to freight. We hear of trans-oceanic air freight, and such air freight is a big issue. We also wonder about trucking. If trucking had been given a completely free hand, would it have made a difference to our ports? As far as Saint John is concerned, the West Indies has always loomed large to us from an economic trading point of view, and we have had what business there has been from Cuba. What is our position in the future in this regard? These are all questions which have to be answered. I quote from the Ottawa Journal of recent date with reference to this matter;
Perhaps Saint John is but the victim of our geography; a geography which, left to itself, ordains that Canada's growth must mainly be with our central regions, and beyond these to the west and the Pacific. Nor is it easy to combat geography; to overcome the consequences of resources-or lack of them-in given areas.
Yet Saint John's position, one of the problems of a Canadian nationhood, deserves the thought of all of us. For a land half prosperous and half poor is hardly the stuff of greatness.
We in the maritimes, Mr. Speaker, realize that we cannot stop the inevitable, as I said in my opening remarks. This is a request for the full, ungarnished facts. We want the cold truth so that we will know where our future lies. The people there, I am sure, will accept as we have in the past, certain facts of life, and go from there in co-operation with government to different or even related activities. This has been demonstrated on many


previous occasions, and certainly a challenge such as this can be met with our usual forthrightness.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that I represent a riding which is interested in harbour development, I welcome this opportunity of stressing with all hon. members the importance of harbours throughout Canada and the impact of their operation on our economy.
The hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) is worried about the harbours of the maritimes and his concern is due to winter navigation on the St. Lawrence river.
The hon. member for Saint John-Albert does not seem to share the views expressed by his former Conservative colleague, the former minister of transport, Hon. George Hees, at the annual dinner of the dominion marine association and of the lake carriers association held at Montebello on January 22, 1958. Speaking of aids to navigation, Mr. Hees stated that it was possible for certain ships to ply the St. Lawrence in winter and he had this to say:
Thanks to those ships, practically all needs should be met within a few years in the St. Lawrence river and the gulf districts, including the winter navigation that might be possible in the various ports of the lower St. Lawrence and even in Quebec harbour.
The hon. member for Saint John-Albert must not have appreciated either the statement made by his Conservative colleague, the present member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), minister of transport in the previous Conservative government, who on January 4, 1962, delivered a speech about winter navigation.
The January 5, 1962 issue of La Presse published an item about the official opening of winter navigation in Three Rivers, in which Hon. Leon Balcer was reported as having said;
The federal government will endeavour to encourage shipping as far as the port of Three Elvers, because such an activity will promote to large extent the economic development not only of the Three Rivers area but of the whole country.
The hon. member for Saint John-Albert was a member of this house in 1958 and in 1962, and we never heard him complain to his two colleagues who were ministers of transport from 1957.
To reassure the hon. member for Saint John-Albert about his fears concerning prosperity of maritime ports, I will quote him a few figures which are an indication of the prosperity of these ports. Reviewing statistics published by the national harbours board, we can see that the gains in tonnage for the port of Saint John, show an increase of

82 per cent in 1960 compared to 1959, an increase of 14 per cent in 1961 over 1960 and a slight decrease in 1962.
Concerning the port of Halifax, it maintained the same tonnage in 1960 and 1961; in 1962, the tonnage increased by 7 per cent.
Those figures indicate that, at the present time, the ports of Halifax and Saint John are not only maintaining their operations but are experiencing an increase in tonnage for import and export goods, even though during the winter navigation on the St. Lawrence has increased.
Hon. members realize that the Department of Transport's icebreaker service must ensure winter navigation on the St. Lawrence so that merchant ships may proceed on the lower St. Lawrence and in the gulf itself.
It is imperative for the industrial development of the north shore that ships carrying ore, paper and aluminum from nearby plants to the United States and Europe stop over in centres like Port Cartier, Seven Islands and Baie Comeau.
The south shore will one day be more industrialized than it is at present. Assistance should be given by both the federal and provincial governments to that economically underdeveloped area to attract new industries. Communities like Chandler, Perce, Ri-mouski and Riviere du Loup will require water transportation facilities all year round.
The co-operation of icebreakers is also required to assist the ferryboats which ply between the north shore and the south shore of the St. Lawrence, as well as the small coasting vessels which give the service between the neighbouring ports of the lower St. Lawrence and the north shore of the gulf, in order that, in the absence of a railway, those centres may be supplied and may ship the goods produced by the local industries.
For a few years, European and Canadian shipyards have been building boats reinforced to such a degree that they can resist to navigation amidst the floating ice. Some of those ships have gone upstream and reached the ports of Quebec and Three Rivers, thus promoting our imports and exports at a reduced rate for the cost of transportation. Such reinforced boats resort to icebreakers when they find deep ice, but they can navigate without help in the regions covered with floating ice or thin ice.
Above Three Rivers and up to Montreal, the icebreakers are in service to prevent the floods caused by ice piling up along the shore and in the channel. Therefore, the icebreakers are called upon to prevent such ice jams.
Winter Navigation on St. Lawrence
After all, winter shipping on the St. Lawrence river is done thanks to the icebreakers, reinforced ships, coasters and ferryboats which are essential in order to supply and ensure the economic life of certain areas along the river.
The hon. member for Saint John-Albert which are essential in order to supply and inquiry and study the shipping situation all across Canada. I do not think that an inquiry is necessary. This government has set up two boards which are certainly aware of this problem, the Atlantic development board and the national economic development board.
These two national agencies, following research and surveys, will be in a position to make recommendations for the continuation by the Canadian ports of their operations on the present scale and for an increase of their yearly volume of goods.
Science progress and the development of new industrial areas will ensure an increased traffic in our Canadian ports, and all the areas served by harbours should be able to take advantage of these benefits.
I hope that all our national ports will share in the economic growth of our country and that governments at all levels, as well as private industry, will provide them with the necessary funds in order to meet their objectives, that is economic prosperity and stability.

We should like to support the motion advanced by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) while expressing some regret that the hon. member who has just spoken from the government side should have given us what is almost the traditional answer-"Why didn't you do something about it when you were in power?"
The hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel) interjects: "He did not say that". I am paraphrasing what I think was the effect of what the hon. member was saying. I stand corrected if I gave the impression that he said so in those exact words.
Part (b) of the motion would, of course, be very difficult, I imagine, for any board of inquiry to analyse and develop, but I certainly agree very much with what is stated in parts (a) and (c). I have brought up this subject on a number of occasions in previous parliaments, as I think the hon. member for Saint John-Albert will probably remember. One of my reasons for doing so, and I should probably be somewhat ashamed about it, was that it was guaranteed to start some kind of argument because, obviously, the interests of the maritime members, particularly of those

Winter Navigation on St. Lawrence members who represent Halifax and Saint John, are strongly affected by developments on the St. Lawrence.
It was obvious to me that there were some differences of opinion within the previous government with regard to the gradual development of icebreaking services and other aids to winter navigation which were being pushed forward by the Department of Transport. I feel there was a marked tendency for people in politics to speak differently in different parts of the country in connection with this controversy. I have always felt there should be a consistency in approaching this problem. My personal feeling is that the Department of Transport has, under instruction, gone out of its way to assist in the development of winter navigation on the St. Lawrence and I believe the people in the maritimes have had every right to complain about this, since it has not been stated in a context which had regard to the interests and facilities they have.
I recall that on one occasion when I brought this question up in a debate in this house I was told by a government employee who is an authority on shipping that there would be a saving of approximately $20 a ton on the freight of everything brought into Montreal or Quebec in the wintertime, compared with having it go to Halifax or Saint John first. This figure in itself, given to me by a government employee, was argument enough to convince me that this matter ought to be examined very thoroughly.
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Saint John-Albert for having brought this question to the attention of the house and I hope the government will consider accepting his suggestion that there should be such an inquiry. Among other things it would, if adopted, remove this extremely controversial subject from the tricks that can be played with it by people pushing a partisan point of view.
If I might speak on a side issue for a few moments, I should like to say to the hon. member for Saint John-Albert-and this has to do with his suggestion to the house that I was unfair to maritime members-that if he would look at the script of my remarks he would see that their substance is somewhat different from the story which ran in the newspapers. The main point of my remarks- and they have a relation to the problem which is before us now-was to the effect that the maritime members of parliament are often kept so busy by their constituents chasing constituency matters that they do not have time to work on the larger issues within the national framework which relate to their region. I am delighted that in this particular

instance the hon. member for Saint John-Albert has, in a sense, given the lie to that particular interpretation. But, if it is any consolation to him, he will find that in my remarks I made particular reference to him as one of the exceptions.
As to the way in which this inquiry could be carried out, I should like to suggest that this subject is of sufficient importance as to warrant an inquiry of the kind suggested in the motion before us. I am very doubtful about any promise by the Minister of Transport to have it examined by a departmental committee. It seems to me this would really not get anywhere. I should not like to have it examined by a departmental committee because it seems to me we really would not get anywhere. On the other hand, I should not like it to have the status of a full royal commission in the sense that I think this would perhaps blow the matter up beyond an economic analysis and the development of a strictly alternative transportation policy. For that reason we believe this is a good motion and we would hope that the government would consider accepting it. It certainly seems to me that it was presented in the best of spirits and it is worth real consideration.
