speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on this question eagerly because there is no matter of greater interest to me or, indeed, to the city of Halifax and its economy than the question of the continuing inroads on our port traffic being made not only by winter navigation but also by the St. Lawrence seaway, and the diversion of so much Canadian exports and imports through United States ports to points of destination or from points of origin in Ontario and the west.
I speak in support of the principle of the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) and I compliment him on his thorough approach and research on the matter. I say that I support the resolution in principle because it is my understanding that the Atlantic development board is already undertaking such an investigation, and I feel that this is the proper board to supervise, if not to carry out, an investigation of this type.
Before going into the question of winter navigation, may I say I regret that the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) did not consider the (b) part of the resolution of great importance, because I feel that it is. Before confederation was consummated, indeed as far back as 1851, Joseph Howe in his memorable speech at Southampton, as did all other Nova Scotian people contemplating confederation, spoke of the consequences of our port and the ports of Nova Scotia and

New Brunswick generally becoming winter ports for Canada. This was agreed upon as part of the spirit of confederation. Perhaps I will return to that a little later.
I agree with the sentiment expressed by the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) when he hopes that our commerce will develop in such a way that the economy of each and every port in Canada will greatly improve; but with all deference to him I cannot agree with the statistics he quotes regarding total tonnage in the ports of Saint John and Halifax. The hon. member quotes tonnage figures for the port of Halifax as being unchanged from 1960 to 1961 and showing a slight increase in 1962. But he has dealt with the question of gross tonnage, and gross tonnage has increased only because of an increase in oil and gypsum products being handled which, while they inflate the total tonnage, provide little in the way of manhours of employment on the waterfront. I have had occasion to say previously in the house that it is packaged general cargo, the type that the longshoreman has to swing his hook into, which provides employment to labour on the waterfront.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INQUIRY INTO WINTER NAVIGATION ON ST. LAWRENCE
speechtext:
I am very pleased that honest disagreements can at times take place within our party. The problem in the port of Halifax and also in the port of Saint John is that general cargo decreased all during the Tory years in office and during the years of increasing icebreaking activities on the St. Lawrence, and this has resulted in a very serious unemployment situation on our waterfronts.
I think that the question of winter navigation can be approached from two beginnings. First, I do not believe that, economically, winter navigation on the St. Lawrence is a good thing. I do not think it is a good thing at all, but I think that we in the maritimes are broadminded enough to recognize that some increasing measure of winter navigation on the St. Lawrence is inevitable. I say it is not a good thing because let us remember that navigation in the winter on the St. Lawrence does not create any new commerce. It merely takes away trade from the Atlantic
Winter Navigation on St. Lawrence ports and transfers it to the St. Lawrence ports, which already enjoy a prosperous summer trade. If you accept the premise that the St. Lawrence ports and port workers are already more prosperous, then surely we must reach the conclusion that the use of government funds to expand winter navigation on the St. Lawrence at the expense of the Atlantic ports is a policy of robbing the poor to help the rich.
Not only has our gross packaged cargo tonnage not increased during the past six years, but at the same time the tonnage in the St. Lawrence ports of Three Rivers, Montreal and so on has increased sharply. The natural growth of our population and of our economy alone should have resulted in some increase in the volume being handled through the Atlantic ports, but this has not been the case.
Having accepted as being to some degree inevitable the proposition that winter navigation will continue to exist, I say that the position of the maritime provinces is that we must have a more realistic freight rate structure so that our ports can compete. This matter was touched on by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, and I am in wholehearted agreement with him in this respect. After all, much of the freight being imported or exported through maritime ports is hauled by the government-owned railway to or from those ports, and if the railway is not fully utilized it will build up a larger deficit than otherwise. This railway always operates at a deficit, and I cannot see that there is much national wisdom or economic gain from a national point of view in using the St. Lawrence ports as the result of great expenditure of public funds to keep these ports open in the winter, when as a consequence you cause railwaymen to be laid off and the railways to have less revenue and a larger deficit because goods are not being transported by the railway to or from the maritime ports.
I think this last point is more particularly significant inasmuch as we do not have a Canadian merchant marine at the present time. We are therefore left in the position that the money involved in the transporting of goods from central Canada to a point on the ocean equivalent to Halifax or Saint John, and the wages earned by the seamen involved, go outside of the nation and are lost. It goes to foreign owned ships, and the wages go to foreign seamen, whereas if the goods are shipped through Atlantic ports in the wintertime our railways remain more prosperous. This surely is of interest to our nation, and in addition it is Canadians who receive employment.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that at the present time under the Maritimes Freight Rates Act,

Winter Navigation on St. Lawrence no subsidies are paid on goods imported or exported through the Atlantic ports. I suggest that we certainly need to undertake a revision of our freight rates structure. If this were done, and if for every dollar spent on icebreaking and allied activities in the St. Lawrence a similar amount were spent by way of subsidies on freight rates, then we would again be in a position to compete. As I have said before, no ship owner in the world will risk a vessel on the St. Lawrence during winter, despite icebreaking activities, if he can ship through the ports of Halifax or Saint John at no extra cost.
Earlier I said that it was part of the agreement under which the maritimes went into confederation that we would have this wintertime business, that we would be the winter ports of Canada. I would remind hon. members on all sides of the house, particularly those from Ontario and Quebec, that when they talk about the spirit of confederation, the undertakings of confederation, they must also remember that the maritimes were given these undertakings.

If Quebec wishes to remain faithful to the spirit of the British North America Act, may I remind that province of the reasons and motives that led the maritimes to enter confederation.
ITextt
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that we have not even received the gain in cargo that should have come about as a result of the natural growth in population and the natural growth in commerce. Our package cargo has actually decreased in volume and we have suffered losses in our winter business. They have been made more severe because we have been steadily losing business in the summertime to the St. Lawrence seaway.
I cannot agree that this house should undertake this investigation, because it is being undertaken by the Atlantic development board, the group that can best deal with this matter. Nevertheless I would urge the government to pay strict attention to these investigations and give very serious consideration to a new national freight rate structure. I do not believe this structure should be of the postage stamp type, which would enable anyone to ship commodities from one point in Canada to another at the same charge. However, the system adopted should be a little closer to the postage stamp type of freight toll, and then we in the maritimes would have an opportunity to share in the prosperity of the rest of Canada.

speechtext:
It was my privilege many years ago, Mr. Speaker, to unite


the efforts of the cities of Halifax and Saint John in solving a problem which this house and its ministers had been unable to solve for many years. I refer to the subject of taxation on crown properties. We began with railway properties in Halifax and Saint John, and, following that, we evolved a municipal grants system in Canada.
I am in the fortunate position, Mr. Speaker, of not knowing what happened prior to April 8 and I am not burdened with concern about what I may have said before that date. On the contrary, I am concerned with something of a more vital nature. Until recently I happened to be a member of the port commission of the city of Halifax, while acting also in another official capacity. This brought me into very close touch with the problems of Saint John and Halifax, vis-a-vis the national government and its policies in respect of navigation on the St. Lawrence.
It might be well if I were to recall briefly something of the anatomy of winter navigation which was put together by the port commission some time ago. For many years it was customary for practically all movements on the river to cease some time early in December, until some time about the middle of April. This was known as the closed as opposed to the open season. During the closed season the only exception to the general paralysis seems to have been the cross-river ferries, the flood control operations of the icebreakers working from the Quebec bridge to above Three Rivers, and a small commercial movement from Pointe au Pic where, if the winds were right, there was usually sufficient open water for coasting vessels to serve north shore points to the east which had no other transportation or connection with the outside world.
During this period between December and April the St. Lawrence river, in so far as export and import cargoes were concerned, was closed. Such cargoes between Canada and other countries were loaded and discharged at Halifax or Saint John. It cannot be over-emphasized that it was upon this condition that the major portion of the business of the Atlantic ports was based. Indeed, it was in part on this condition that the arguments for the maritime provinces to enter confederation were based and were accepted, as my colleague so well pointed out a few moments ago. This house frequently hears references to constitutional obligations under confederation. We have our obligations to which we are asking this house, from time to time, to have a sense of responsibility. I would hope that we could all forgo them. We would be willing to forgo them if there were new ways of doing things and

better understanding between the peoples of this great nation. When we hear this talk about constitutional rights, we must remind people that we have them too. Indeed, all parts of Canada have them.
We, in the maritimes, believe it is a good thing to look at the problems of the other fellow through his eyes from time to time. We think that this is a practice that might be observed occasionally in this house, and indeed throughout other parts of Canada. It might bear benefits to all the Canadian people. I mentioned earlier the anatomy of shipping policy, but we now find that certain changes have occurred. We find that flood control operations have extended to the lower shore, with its natural resources. We do not criticize that whatever. We see this gradual increase in icebreaking services up the river. We recognize this is a national development; but we also know that none of those costs are being included in the charges against ship users. This is a public service. This is not economically sound.
One result of the increased federal government subsidies and services to open up a new route of transportation has been to destroy our competitive position. We say, therefore, the Canadian government definitely has an obligation to correct this growing imbalance in our competitive position.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, perhaps some people do not realize the extent to which the Atlantic development board has already gone in recognizing the plea for action on this matter.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) is making some suggestion, as he has done quite frequently. I would be glad to answer him when the opportunity presents itself, but right now we have more important business to deal with.
Briefly the situation is that you have a conflict of interests in the Atlantic provinces with the sincere and well-motivated interests of the people along the St. Lawrence river, and you can only resolve such a conflict of interests in the light of the most exacting study of the justification of the claims of both. It cannot be resolved by a debate across the floor of the House of Commons.
This problem confronted the former minister of transport in the same way as it now confronts the present minister, and it cannot be solved in any way other than within the principle of a scheme of organization such as that proposed by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell). However, I think it must be recognized that the Atlantic development board now has the staff and skill to do
Winter Navigation on St. Lawrence the essential research work that is basic to an intelligent decision regarding the kind of policy that must ensue, and that will work in the mutual interests of both areas.
I understand the board has two gentlemen who are skilled in these fields and who would be able to define the nature and scope of the problem. Having defined the nature and scope of it, the board will then be able to get people together who are not biased in favour of either the Atlantic ports or the St. Lawrence ports, and who will be able to make an objective examination of this critical problem.
To some people, on the face of it winter navigation is sheer economic nonsense. Some have gone so far as to say that; but on the other hand there are those along the St. Lawrence who say the economic development of Canada demands the maximum utilization of this great seaway. We feel, however, that the case has not yet been fully justified by those who support the St. Lawrence development.
I believe that the principle and objectivity sought by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert can be assured by the steps now taken by the Atlantic development board in putting together personnel on a team who will view the problem objectively, report to the minister, and through him to the house. In that way we can achieve a realistic policy that will be in the interests of both areas.

subtopic: *TRIP TO WINDSOR BY EXTERNAL AFFAIRS MINISTER
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INQUIRY INTO WINTER NAVIGATION ON ST. LAWRENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we heard many views exchanged this afternoon on that ever ticklish matter of winter navigation. As far as I am concerned, you know where I stand; I represent the Quebec South riding. You know how much this matter of winter navigation was discussed in Quebec these last few years. This afternoon, I would not want anyone to think that I am speaking in any capacity other than that of hon. member for Quebec South.
Having heard the version given in this house by the hon. members from the maritimes, I think the question should be first considered in its constitutional context and then in its economic aspect.
I think and I agree with my hon. friends that the matter, in its constitutional context, must be discussed with the same objectivity as any other matter concerning the constitution of our country. When we talk about reshaping our constitution, I think we will have to take into consideration the examples given this afternoon.
Now, as far as the economic aspect is concerned, the solution advocated by this government is to charge the new Atlantic

Inquiries of the Ministry economic council with the requested investigation. I think that council will have in its hands all the tools, all the required information and will get in contact with every profession and every person interested in this great problem. I am sure that on the basis of their investigation we can get very happy results.
Of course, at the time the maritimes entered confederation, it must be recognized that we had transportation systems other than those in use today. Transportation is improving every day and we must reconsider our transportation system, not at the expense of some people but to the advantage of all.
In that particular field, I was reading, a few weeks ago, that the United States are presently considering the feasibility of keeping the St. Lawrence seaway open 12 months a year.
If, thanks to modern technology, we find ways and means to improve navigation and expand its volume, I feel that we might then draw the blueprint for a new policy which would not discriminate against anyone, but would be to the general advantage.
Mr. Speaker, I am confident that through an exchange of objective viewpoints, and with the necessary good will on every part, we shall be able to find in this country of ours a place for everyone, and that all Canadians will benefit thereby.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EXPENSE ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS AND SENATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to my hon. friend for raising this interesting point. I should explain that under the recent amendment the expense allowances are paid quarterly, whereas previously they were paid on an annual basis. In connection with the Senate allowances, the chief treasury officer, after consultation with the Clerk of the Senate and on his advice, was of the opinion that the recent amendment permitted the payment of the residual portion of the smaller allowance of $2,000 per annum which applied from January 1 to April 7 to be paid on September 30; that is, at the end of the quarter. The chief treasury officer for the House of Commons, on the other hand, was of the opinion that the amendment w the Senate and House of Commons Act did not affect the operation of the former provision in so far as the period from January 1 to April 7 was concerned. He accordingly declined to make payment of the allowances for that period before the end of the year.
Section 31(6) of the Financial Administration Act provides that where the comptroller is of the opinion that a doubt exists as to the legality or otherwise of a proposed charge to an appropriation provided for the expenses of the Senate or the House of Commons, he shall report through the Minister of Finance to the appropriate minister, who shall obtain a decision in accordance with such procedure as may from time to time

Interim Supply
be prescribed. It is my understanding that this would be the internal economy committees of the respective chambers.
As there is in the opinion of the comptroller a doubt existing as to whether these allowances may or may not be paid at the present time for the period January 1 to April 7, this matter is being drawn to the attention of the Speakers of the House of Commons and of the Senate. I have written to them and suggested that they get together and obtain legal advice, and perhaps we may straighten out the point which the hon. member was so kind as to bring to my attention.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, since the committee on privileges and elections is supposed to sit tonight, I do not intend to speak at great length on interim supply.
If I take part in the debate tonight, it is not because we merely want to kill time, as was suggested these last few days. Such is not the case at all. I have some facts to bring to the attention of the house which mainly concern my riding, and I take the opportunity of this interim supply motion to point out to the house some of the facts that clearly show to what extent the present administration and the previous one have placed the country in an untenable position. Besides, the present government is aware of it now. As a matter of fact, one realizes it readily to see the government act.
Even though Canada is a very rich country with a very high production and producing capacity, our people have great needs, as evidenced by the large number of depressed areas, such as my own riding of Abitibi in northwestern Quebec.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I suggest to hon. members that their conversations in the house make it extremely difficult for other members, including the chairman, to follow the speech now being made by the hon. member for Chapleau?

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
The government is slow in answering the plea of the people for the right to benefit from the wealth which now exists. That only goes to show that the Liberal party was not ready to take over last April. Ready to levy taxes, yes, but not to administer the country.
Tax increases lead us to believe that the government is concerned about the annual deficits which are reaching astronomical proportions, and the people of this country as well as its business and industrial leaders are also worried about them.
The government is aware of present needs, but its actions are paralysed by a lack of funds. Taxes do not bring in enough money to balance the budget, and the government knows how unpopular taxes are. That is surely why the government and especially the Department of National Revenue, since last spring in particular, have been constantly pestering the taxpayers in my riding.
As a matter of fact, since last spring, income tax inspectors from the Rouyn district office have not stopped making cuts on the receipts for charitable donations contained in the income tax returns of certain people. I

say certain people because there is apparently some discrimination in some working-class areas of my constituency.
Indeed, while in some cases receipts for charitable donations are being cut from $372 to $150 without reason, letters are written to the Rouyn office, information is sought to find out where, when and how the investigations were made. And in this regard, last June 5, I received the following reply from the office of the director of income tax:
We can assure you that we have not reduced the amounts specified for charitable donations without prior investigation.
I asked again where and when those investigations had been made and by whom. Here is the reply I got on August 27, 1963, from the chief assessment officer in the district income tax office:
We draw your attention to the fact that in the case under consideration, under section 133 (1) of the Income Tax Act, the employees of the division are not authorized to give information to a third party.
Mr. Chairman, that third party was the member for Chapleau who wanted to know where and when the investigations mentioned had been made, and it seems there is no way of finding that out, but it still holds true just the same that some workers, some miners see their receipts for charitable donations cut while other miners, other workers, who have practically the same revenue, the same salary and the same dependants, see their income tax return and their receipts for charitable donations accepted in full.
Consequently, it makes one wonder if there is not some kind of patronage granted to some taxpayers, and people are wondering in my riding if that is not a kind of punishment for some.
Mr. Chairman, I protest against the action taken by inspectors of the income tax office in Rouyn and I ask the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Garland) to put a stop to that situation and to find, with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), another way to finance government operations. I urge him to study carefully the suggestions made by the Social Credit party and to give back to the Bank of Canada the role it must play in our country's economy. Mr. Chairman, I want to talk about another matter in this chamber, that is television.
National radio and television is not available in all parts of my riding. I know that Chapleau is a sprawling riding, but I am also aware that it is relatively easy to bring radio and television services everywhere. I do not think that there is some insurmountable physical obstacle. In fact, private industry has managed to make television broadcasts available in the towns of Chibougamau
Interim Supply
and Chapais but at an exorbitant cost. Consequently, physical obstacles are not insurmountable since private industry did it. Thus it is only a matter of financial limitations which prevent the broadcasting of radio and television programs.
In this regard, I should like to refer to a case which is typical of the mining area of Chibougamau and Chapais, where some 2,000 families must pay $200 for the television cable and $6 a month payable a year in advance, that is a total sum of $272 before enjoying T.V. services that the majority of Canadians in other sections of the country enjoy free of charge. And yet the miners from Chibougamau and Chapais pay taxes and they may be the highest per capita in the country.
The Minister of Finance should make available to C.B.C. a larger budget so that it may satisfy the wishes of the citizens from those communities, such as Parent and Clova, which are scattered along the C.N.R. tracks or, in the meantime, he should grant the corporation some funds so that the rental of the television cable may be reduced and the poor as well as the rich in the towns of Chibougamau and Chapais may enjoy television broadcasts.
At the present time, the mining area of Chibougamau and Chapais is served for television purposes through Saguenay-Lake St. John. And yet, this mining area is actually in the political riding of Chapleau. I am of the opinion that it is irregular to give television service through an area not politically connected with the area to be served. The same thing was done for the railway service. A railroad was started in direction of the Lake St. John area.
Again, when time came to build a road for cars and trucks, a dirt road, the same thing was done; the Saguenay-Lake St. John was the first to be served.
Mr. Chairman, please note that I am not at all jealous of the fact that the Saguenay-Lake St. John was the first to be connected to this mining area, but I find it quite strange that, in order to develop an area, the first thing done is to provide exits to another area.
Consequently, I urge the C.B.C. to take immediately the necessary steps to give the citizens of Chibougamau and Chapais radio and television services at a price comparable to other parts of the country.
Mr. Chairman, people complain about unemployment which has been prevailing for a long time in our area and which not only reduces and cripples trade and industry but also brings about undeserved poverty and concern in many families thereby affected.
And yet, those numerous families suffer from privation, not because we lack things

Interim Supply
in this country, but rather because they need things that exist. And if those needs are not satisfied, it is rather due to the fact that they lack purchasing power.
Mr. Chairman, when we see the advertising which is done now to sell things, to sell goods produced by Canadians, we may ask why, in a country known as the richest in the world, it is still necessary to collect old clothes to dress poor children who want to go to school in some areas called "underdeveloped" or "emergency areas".
And concerning that matter, I want to speak about Chapleau county, in Abitibi, which is designated as such an area at the present time, amid plenty and surpluses. In fact, people there are still in that condition where they have to collect old clothes to enable children to attend school, in order to take advantage of the opportunity to get an education which they need.
Mr. Chairman, in order to enable those citizens to get the things offered to them in quantity in all ways, and in quality, the government should use the Bank of Canada to coin production and services offered in surpluses, and distribute them, in the form of dividends, to all Canadian citizens, because everyone, in one way or another, has taken part in the production of goods and services in this country.
Mr. Chairman, the Canadian government should not be so mean when it comes to paying a retirement pension to our senior citizens, and I am of the opinion that the present retirement pension should begin immediately at 65 years, without any test, and at 60 for people without any resources.
Mr. Chairman, I cannot see why those in need would not be able to benefit from the production and resources of this country without taking anything away from the people who work, or depriving others from part of their income.
Mr. Chairman, I maintain that old age pensions, retirement pensions, old age assistance pensions, pensions for the blind or the disabled, family allowances, and all similar social welfare measures, should be financed by the Bank of Canada. The necessary funds could be drawn from the production surplus we accumulate year after year, that is, the unsold surpluses.
We must allow the Bank of Canada to play the part it was created to play, and it behooves the government to instruct it to play that part.

To date, Mr. Chairman, my interventions in the discussion never contributed at all to any inconvenience for the Chair and, therefore, I can sum up my remarks in compliance with the traditional procedures.

Congratulations to those who carry out those functions; they do it in all fairness and with a sense of responsibility which is all to their credit.
Mr. Chairman, as a representative for a riding which made a tremendous contribution to the development of several neighbouring areas through many sacrifices, during a few centuries of history, I should like to take this opportunity now offered to me to call the attention of the house to the need to adopt an attitude more consistent with the needs and the purposes of the people in our region and of all Canadians in general who showed, by their labour and their sense of sacrifice that the sources of courage, of good will and of generous dispositions are far from exhausted so long as they are given a chance through legislation which allows for a reasonable proportion of economic realities.
All Canadians still wish to participate in the development of their country. To be effective, that participation must involve the essential elements of security and of proper freedom for one and all.
The implementation, as soon as possible, of appropriate public works in order to alleviate unemployment in our region is absolutely necessary and would be greatly appreciated. The decisions taken by the government to designate the so-called distressed areas will have to be altered to take into account the needs of our region.
During the month of September, in the course of a regular meeting of the municipal corporation of Kamouraska county, in which nearly all the mayors of the municipalities in the county took part, a resolution was passed and a copy thereof was forwarded to the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) and his colleague, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mac-Eachen), asking them to include the county of Kamouraska in the list of those which can benefit from a federal grant for unemployment works and from a tax cut for industries wishing to settle in the county.
During the last week of the month of September, the members of the chamber of commerce of St. Pascal, Kamouraska county, of which I am a member, also adopted a similar resolution. I hope the ministers will take those requests into consideration and that appropriate decisions will be taken so that the county of Kamouraska will get from this government the share of benefits it can rightfully expect.
Quite a number of these plans could be carried into effect without delay; some studies have been completed, various programs have been referred to the authorities several years ago, but their implementation

often seems to be paralysed through a lack of agreement and co-operation between the central and provincial governments.
We hope that the necessary decisions will be arrived at as soon as possible by the responsible authorities, for in Kamouraska and elsewhere, people have had enough of all these discussions and, quite naturally, expect action.
The same thing applies to the implementation of the ARDA program, and to the generous distribution of subsidies to farmers. It is true that Kamouraska county is not included among the depressed areas, but let us not forget that due to the prevailing economic conditions more than 30 per cent of our citizens depend on social welfare services for their livelihood.
The constant worry created by a financial system which functions contrary to present economic realities has led us to a way of life which is truly upside-down.
Too many are those who are attracted by the moon while entire families still have to go without the necessities of life. We no longer have enough room in our jails for criminals, most of whom have taken to that kind of life because of a lack of guidance. Not only is society responsible for that state of affairs but it must take the necessary steps as soon as possible to correct a situation it contributed to create.

We know that consumption is the object of production. That it would be useless to make shoes if people were not to wear them. That houses have no value whatsoever unless people live in them. That food will perish unless it is consumed.

Lack of confidence paralyses our action, and instead of using our plentiful resources, we always have shortages. Any progress, scientific discovery and invention originate in the human mind.

He wanted to dispense with the province of Quebec co-operative societies paying an additional amount on those bushels of grain to the Canadian wheat board, to the western farmers.
Mr. Chairman, there are in the province of Quebec as well as in the other provinces a great number of farmers whose lands are presently encumbered with farm loans, lands that were nevertheless free of debt for generations, that were cleared by the ancestors of today's occupants. That is the present situation, although some claim our economy is sound whereas the farmers' lands are mortgaged to the hilt to either the federal or the provincial farm loan boards.
Mr. Chairman, such a situation depends only on one thing. We cannot charge that all the farmers are poor managers, that they are imbeciles, that they know nothing about production. I believe that there are some farmers who can produce much more than some members of parliament. It is not up to us to judge them. We should seek here at home the reason for this state of affairs. Is it our laws, our own administration in this house which force those farmers to mortgage their farms?

Mr. Chairman, it is not by lending more to the farmers through farm loans that we shall resolve the problem. What the farmer wishes presently is to obtain a better price for his products and to pay a little less in taxation. Thus, the farmers may succeed in making both ends meet. Mr. Chairman, there is another point I should like to deal with; it concerns our young people, unemployment, unemployment insurance, but also the economic development of this country. And at this stage of my remarks, I would ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) to listen carefully to what I am going to say.
I want to deal with the problem facing our young people today when they wish to join the armed forces and benefit from federal government assistance. When a student wants to join the armed forces, he is paid a salary, given military training, clothed, lodged and fed. But when the same student wants to get a scholarship to go to university, he is told: "Wait a minute, the government does not give scholarships".
How is it that the government has money to give our young men military training, but have absolutely nothing to offer to those who want to carry on their studies at the university?
Mr. Chairman, one must not forget that our university students can defend our country as well as our young military trainees, for every man defends his country in his own way.
Now, why does not the government give direct assistance to those who want to carry on their studies at the university, as it does in the case of those who wish to join the army?
It is all very well to defend our country, but we must not only defend it, we should also develop it, and those who will develop it will be perhaps in as good a position to defend it as those who will have had military training.
Everybody could work along the same lines, some looking after the country's military defense while others would look after its growth.
Mr. Chairman, that is the point I wished to raise about youth. I know that the Minister of National Health and Welfare takes a special interest in the young people of Canada, since she has already started a campaign and made sacrifices herself by giving up smoking. That is already a good example she has set our young people in order to keep them in good health.
I am asking the government whether they have a solution, as quite often they have not, why-

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, could we be informed of the friendly agreement that seems to exist between the member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) and the leader of the house?
Mr. Chairman, it is always better to have friends than enemies.
So the divorce is over.

Mr. Chairman, I did not get the question or the remarks of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montealm (Mr. Pigeon) but if they are in any way similar to his other remarks I will not lose any time in trying to reply to them.
In conclusion I would simply suggest to the government, seeing that they are unable to solve the problem of unemployment, misery, hunger and insecurity in our country at present, and have not found any solution in their own political structure, after 95 years of trial and errors, that they should change their routine and try some other means, like the monetary reform advocated by the Social Credit party. You may call that "funny money" but instead of calling the Social Credit monetary system the "funny money" system you should examine your own financial systems when you have to devaluate the dollar, when you have a revaluated or devaluated dollar. That never happened under a Social Credit administration because there never was one, but it happened under the Liberal and Conservative administrations.
At the present time we need solutions to wipe out the national debt which is increasing day by day and to remedy unemployment, misery and hunger.
I am asking the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and their colleagues in the various departments to consider the solutions offered by Social Credit; they may find solutions to the problems they have to face at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate your giving me the floor at this moment. The hour is getting late and I would like to appeal to every hon. member of the house to appreciate the circumstances under which we are presently operating, and to understand something on principle and not on expediency. I ask, right now, will all hon. members and all parties agree to call all speeches to a complete halt and vote on the important issue before us?
Anyone who stands now is guilty of denial of principle and expediency. May we now, sir, have the vote?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to know from the house leader, now that the hurricane warnings have been taken down, what business will be ready for the ship of state tomorrow, on the calmer seas?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I sincerely hope that the hon. gentleman's forecast is correct and that the hurricanes are over, both in the Caribbean and here. We would go ahead tomorrow with the old age pensions bill, the two Northwest Territories bills and the vocational training resolution. That, I think, would probably occupy the greater part of the day. If there were any time left the government would reserve the right to take anything on the order paper of a relatively non-controversial character.
